Dictionary search

Source: vignettes/dict-search.Rmd
dict-search.Rmd

search_dict() matches a vocabulary list against a sentence corpus and returns hits with standardized term names. This vignette pairs textpress’s built-in dict_political – surface variants like “GOP” or “MAGA” mapped to canonical labels – with a small dictionary of policy issues, runs both over politics coverage from the weeks after the 2026 midterms, then computes PMI-weighted co-occurrence to see which issues travel with which political labels.

Load packages.

library(textpress)
library(dplyr)
library(DT)

Sources

The corpus comes from two openly reusable sources: the Pew Research Center politics feed, taken from the bundled rss_politics catalog, and The Conversation’s US politics feed. Both allow reuse with attribution (The Conversation publishes under CC BY-ND 4.0; Pew Research Center under its terms of use), so the article text can be saved with this vignette. Entries were retrieved in November 2026, in the weeks after the midterm elections; links to every article are kept in the results.

feeds <- c(
  textpress::rss_politics |>
    filter(source == "Pew Research Center") |>
    pull(url),
  "https://theconversation.com/us/politics/articles.atom"
)

web_urls <- textpress::fetch_rss(feeds) |>
  select(-doc_id) |>
  distinct(url, .keep_all = TRUE)

Web text and sentence split

read_urls() scrapes and parses the article text; nlp_split_sentences() segments each document into analysis-ready sentence rows.

web_text_list <- web_urls |>
  textpress::read_urls(cores = 4)

web_ss <- web_text_list$text |>
  mutate(doc_id = match(url, unique(url))) |>
  relocate(doc_id, .before = 1) |>
  textpress::nlp_split_sentences(by = c("doc_id", "node_id"))

Dictionaries and search

textpress ships with curated dictionaries in a simple two-column shape: variant (the surface form) and TermName (the canonical label). dict_political maps political identity labels (“Democrat”, “GOP”, “progressive”, “MAGA”, etc.). Any table in the same shape works as a dictionary, so we write a small one for the issues that dominated midterm coverage, then stack the two and run a single search.

DT::datatable(
  textpress::dict_political,
  options = list(pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE
)

An issue dictionary in the same variant / TermName shape.

dict_issues <- data.frame(
  variant = c(
    "economy", "economic", "jobs",
    "inflation", "prices", "cost of living", "affordability",
    "immigration", "immigrants", "border", "deportation", "deportations",
    "tariff", "tariffs", "trade",
    "crime", "policing",
    "health care", "Medicaid", "Affordable Care Act", "Obamacare",
    "abortion", "reproductive rights",
    "democracy"
  ),
  TermName = c(
    rep("Economy", 3), rep("Cost of living", 4), rep("Immigration", 5),
    rep("Trade", 3), rep("Crime", 2), rep("Health care", 4),
    rep("Abortion", 2), "Democracy"
  )
)

Stack both dictionaries (with a category), pass all variants to search_dict() once, then join back to get standardized TermName and category. One search covers issues and political labels.

dict_iss <- dict_issues |>
  mutate(variant_lc = tolower(variant), cat = "issue") |>
  select(variant, variant_lc, term_name = TermName, cat)
dict_pol <- textpress::dict_political |>
  mutate(variant_lc = tolower(variant), cat = "affil") |>
  select(variant, variant_lc, term_name = TermName, cat)
stacked_dict <- bind_rows(dict_iss, dict_pol)

Run search_dict() with all variants, then join back to the stacked dictionary to attach canonical term_name and category.

matches <- web_ss |>
  textpress::search_dict(
    by   = c("doc_id", "node_id", "sentence_id"),
    terms = stacked_dict$variant
  ) |>
  left_join(
    stacked_dict |> select(variant_lc, term_name, cat),
    by = c("term" = "variant_lc")
  )
matches |> arrange(id) |> DT::datatable(rownames = F)

Co-occurrence: counts and PMI (issue × affiliation)

Paragraphs that contain both an issue and a political label form (issue, affil) pairs. Paragraphs rather than sentences, because issues and party labels are often mentioned a sentence or two apart. The id returned by search_dict() joins the by columns with dots, so dropping its last part gives the paragraph. We count pairs and compute PMI:

PMI(x,y)=log⁡N⋅nxynx⋅ny\text{PMI}(x, y) = \log \frac{N \cdot n_{xy}}{n_x \cdot n_y}

where NN is total pair count, nxyn_{xy} is joint count, and nxn_x, nyn_y are marginal counts.

para  <- matches |> mutate(id = sub("[.][^.]*$", "", id))
iss   <- para |> filter(cat == "issue") |> distinct(id, issue = term_name)
affil <- para |> filter(cat == "affil") |> distinct(id, affil = term_name)
ids_both <- intersect(iss$id, affil$id)

pairs <- iss |> filter(id %in% ids_both) |>
  inner_join(affil |> filter(id %in% ids_both), by = "id")

n_total  <- nrow(pairs)
count_xy <- pairs |> count(issue, affil, name = "n_xy")
count_x  <- pairs |> count(issue, name = "n_issue")
count_y  <- pairs |> count(affil, name = "n_affil")

cooccur <- count_xy |>
  left_join(count_x, by = "issue") |>
  left_join(count_y, by = "affil") |>
  mutate(pmi = round(log(n_total * n_xy / (n_issue * n_affil)), 2)) |>
  select(issue, affil, n_xy, n_issue, n_affil, pmi) |>
  arrange(desc(n_xy))

DT::datatable(cooccur, options = list(pageLength = 15), rownames = FALSE)

Summary

search_dict() covers vocabulary breadth that regex can’t – every surface form of a concept matched in a single pass, with canonical labels for grouping. Stacking dict_political with a user-written issue dictionary in the same shape gives co-labeled hits across both dimensions in one search; PMI co-occurrence over those paragraphs surfaces which issues and political labels are actually associated in the corpus.
